messages.author: d0936a6280139a7b
messages.subject: Primate line transect survey analysis
parts:
Dear all,

I'm new at Distance Software and I would like to ask you some doubts about how to analyze the data from a line transect survey with Distance software. We collected the data of  moor macaque population in South Sulawesi by walking 1km transect twice. We were recording every time we saw an individual the distance from the transect, furthermore we were recording data about human activity (presence of humans, presence of animals (dogs or cows), logging (area), constructions, agriculture). Now I'm trying to analyze the data with Distance software but I'm struggeling with some issues, and I would be very happy if someone could help with that :). Thanks a lot!

 - We want to analyze if the presence of the human activity has an effect on the population density, is it possible to estimate population density taking in account this data? Is it a good idea to do it by stratification? i.e. stratify the data on "human presence/not presence" or "agriculture/not agriculture". Is is possible to do multi-stratification analysis?

- Is it better to analyze this data (human activity) as "covariates"?

- We have also some problem with the group size. We recorded every time we saw an individual, but we know that we missed some animals every time. We want to add a multiplier to accurate the estimation. We know the mean size of the groups in this species, and we have the number of individuals we saw every time we found a group. We think that adding a multiplier ("c"), where c = proportion of individuals missing, would be a good approach. If we see a mean of 10 individuals per group, and we know that the groups are abouut 40 individuals, we know we are missing 30 individuals each time, so c = 0.75. Do you think it is a good approach?

Thanks a lot for your help and time,
Best, 
Víctor

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Primate line transect survey analysis
parts:
Victor

A good set of questions, I'll address them in sequence.
  • Effect of human activity
    • If you had designed your survey to address this question, then you would have defined strata on the basis of human activity.  You would then have allocated survey effort (transects) into the strata adequately such that you could produce robust estimates of macaque abundance in each stratum.  I'm guessing this was not done at the time of the design, but rather you are considering it post-survey.  The challenge with this is there may be too few transects in some strata of interest to produce reliable estimates.
    • The term "covariates" in distance sampling is usually associated with the idea of modelling the detection function.  While it may be the case that detectability is affected by human activity; you are interested in whether macaque abundance is affected by human activity.  The two are not equivalent.
    • There are other approaches to the assessment of the human activity effect besides stratification you might consider a spatial modelling approach where variables such as distance from village is used as a predictor of encounter rates adjusted for imperfect detectability.  See this paper applied to roe deer: Valente, A.M., Marques, T.A., Fonseca, C. et al. A new insight for monitoring ungulates: density surface modelling of roe deer in a Mediterranean habitat. Eur J Wildl Res 62, 577–587 (2016). MailScanner has detected a possible fraud attempt from "link.getmailspring.com" claiming to be https://doi.org/10.1007/s10344-016-1030-0
  • Multiplier applied to group size
    • I am reluctant to recommend the application of a blanket adjustment factor to your survey data.  I would think the proportion of a group that is undetected would vary quite a bit.  Applying such a large correction factor would swamp any other decisions made in the analysis of your data.  As an alternative, Buckland et al. (2010) suggest recording the detection of each individual encountered, rather than trying to record the number of individuals in the group; analysing the data as detections of individuals rather than groups.  See Buckland, S.T., Plumptre, A.J., Thomas, L. et al. Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates. Int J Primatol 31, 833–847 (2010). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5
I hope some of those suggestions are useful.

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk
The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ

messages.subject: {Disarmed} RE: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Primate line transect survey analysis
parts:
Yes, I would echo Eric’s concerns about the multiplier approach.  You will tend to detect those animals in a group that are closer to the transect, so that you would underestimate the distance from the transect of the group centre.  This will cause you to overestimate abundance – probably by a factor close to your multiplier value.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: {Disarmed} Re: {Disarmed} RE: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] Primate line transect survey analysis
parts:
Victor

As I noted in my earlier reply, the inclusion of covariates in the detection function will provide some indication of whether detectability changes with the covariates included; it does not indicate whether primate abundance changes with the covariates.

Regarding your question about preference for detection function models 1) or 2).  My answer would be "neither".  The fitting of detection functions including covariates is more challenging than fitting detection functions without covariates.  To get a sense of this, I suggest you look at the lecture on covariates in the detection function here:
https://workshops.distancesampling.org/standrews-2019/intro/lectures/BlockH-covariates.pdf
As such, I have seldom encountered studies where more than 3-4 covariates are included in the modelling.  A property called "pooling robustness" ensures that (given g(0)=1), unbiased estimates of abundance are produced even if influential covariates are not included in the detection function model.

Your approach 2) is guaranteed to fail because there are too many covariates and consequently too many parameters to estimate.  Imagine each of your covariates has only two levels, that will result in (I think) an 8 parameter model.  Add more levels to the covariates and the number of parameters to estimate increases.  You will also encounter problems in data sparseness:  how many detections, across what range of detection distances will your data set have for month 1, location 1, animal 1, hactivity 1, logging 1, road 1 and Weather 1?  Likewise for all other covariate combinations.

Best to be very sparing in your use of covariates.  Look at scatterplots of detections or detection distances as functions of month, or logging, or road categories.  That should narrow the number of covariates you entertain for use in your models.

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532
eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk
The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews KY16 9LZ
